# Radon–Nikodym Theorem — proof

**Conventions.** $\nu \ll \mu$ means: $A\in\Sigma$, $\mu(A)=0 \Rightarrow \nu(A)=0$. For measurable $f\ge 0$ (values in $[0,\infty]$) and $A\in\Sigma$, $\int_A f\,d\mu := \int f\mathbf 1_A\,d\mu \in[0,\infty]$. We use the standard facts about integrals of non-negative measurable functions: additivity, monotonicity, the Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT) (hence termwise integration of series of non-negative functions), that $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$ is a measure, that functions equal $\mu$-a.e. have the same integral, and that $\int f\,d\mu<\infty$ implies $f<\infty$ $\mu$-a.e.

**Fact 0.** If $f\ge0$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu=0$ then $\mu(\{f>0\})=0$. Indeed $\frac1m\mu(\{f>1/m\})\le\int f\,d\mu=0$ for each $m$, and $\{f>0\}=\bigcup_m\{f>1/m\}$.

**Step 1 (common finite partition).** Since $\mu,\nu$ are $\sigma$-finite, there are $E_i, F_j\in\Sigma$ with $X=\bigcup_i E_i=\bigcup_j F_j$, $\mu(E_i)<\infty$, $\nu(F_j)<\infty$. The countably many sets $E_i\cap F_j$ cover $X$ and have finite $\mu$- and $\nu$-measure; disjointifying them (replace the $k$-th set $C_k$ by $C_k\setminus\bigcup_{l<k}C_l$) we get pairwise disjoint $X_1,X_2,\dots\in\Sigma$ with $X=\bigsqcup_n X_n$, $\mu(X_n)<\infty$, $\nu(X_n)<\infty$.

## Lemma 1
Let $\alpha,\beta$ be finite measures on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $\alpha(X)>\beta(X)$. Then there is $P\in\Sigma$ with $\alpha(P)>\beta(P)$ and $\alpha(B)\ge\beta(B)$ for all $B\in\Sigma$, $B\subseteq P$.

*Proof.* Put $\sigma(B)=\alpha(B)-\beta(B)\in\mathbb R$. Since both are finite measures, $\sigma$ is countably additive over disjoint sequences (both series converge absolutely), and $\sigma(B)\ge-\beta(X)$. Recursively define $A_0=X$ and, given $A_n\in\Sigma$, let $t_n=\inf\{\sigma(B):B\in\Sigma,\ B\subseteq A_n\}$; then $-\beta(X)\le t_n\le\sigma(\emptyset)=0$. If $t_n=0$ put $B_n=\emptyset$; if $t_n<0$ then $t_n<t_n/2$, so choose $B_n\in\Sigma$, $B_n\subseteq A_n$ with $\sigma(B_n)\le t_n/2$. In both cases $\sigma(B_n)\le t_n/2\le 0$. Put $A_{n+1}=A_n\setminus B_n$.

The $B_n$ are pairwise disjoint ($B_m\subseteq A_m\subseteq A_{n+1}$ is disjoint from $B_n$ for $m>n$). Let $P=\bigcap_n A_n=X\setminus\bigcup_n B_n$. By countable additivity $\sum_n\sigma(B_n)=\sigma(\bigcup_nB_n)$ is a finite real number, and it is a series of non-positive terms, so $\sigma(B_n)\to0$; then $0\ge t_n\ge 2\sigma(B_n)\to0$ gives $t_n\to0$. Now $\sigma(P)=\sigma(X)-\sum_n\sigma(B_n)\ge\sigma(X)>0$, i.e. $\alpha(P)>\beta(P)$. If $B\in\Sigma$, $B\subseteq P$, then $B\subseteq A_n$ for every $n$, so $\sigma(B)\ge t_n$ for all $n$; letting $n\to\infty$, $\sigma(B)\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

## Step 2: existence when $\mu,\nu$ are finite
Assume $\mu(X),\nu(X)<\infty$, $\nu\ll\mu$. Let
$$\mathcal F=\{f:X\to[0,\infty]\ \Sigma\text{-measurable}:\ \textstyle\int_A f\,d\mu\le\nu(A)\ \ \forall A\in\Sigma\}.$$
$0\in\mathcal F$.

*(a) $\mathcal F$ is closed under $\max$.* For $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal F$ and $A\in\Sigma$, let $A_1=A\cap\{f_1\ge f_2\}$, $A_2=A\cap\{f_1<f_2\}$ (measurable, disjoint, union $A$). Then $\int_A\max(f_1,f_2)\,d\mu=\int_{A_1}f_1\,d\mu+\int_{A_2}f_2\,d\mu\le\nu(A_1)+\nu(A_2)=\nu(A)$.

*(b) A maximizer.* Let $s=\sup\{\int_X f\,d\mu:f\in\mathcal F\}\le\nu(X)<\infty$. Pick $f_n\in\mathcal F$ with $\int f_n\,d\mu\to s$ and set $h_n=\max(f_1,\dots,f_n)\in\mathcal F$ (by (a)). $h_n$ increases to a measurable $h$, and $\int f_n\le\int h_n\le s$. By MCT, for every $A$, $\int_A h\,d\mu=\lim\int_A h_n\,d\mu\le\nu(A)$, so $h\in\mathcal F$ and $\int h\,d\mu=s$. Since $\int h\,d\mu<\infty$, $N=\{h=\infty\}$ has $\mu(N)=0$. Let $g_0=h\mathbf 1_{X\setminus N}$: measurable, with values in $[0,\infty)$, equal to $h$ $\mu$-a.e.; hence $\int_A g_0\,d\mu=\int_A h\,d\mu$ for all $A$, so $g_0\in\mathcal F$ and $\int g_0\,d\mu=s$.

*(c) $g_0$ is a density.* Define $\rho(A)=\nu(A)-\int_A g_0\,d\mu$. As $0\le\int_A g_0\,d\mu\le\nu(A)<\infty$ and both $\nu$ and $A\mapsto\int_Ag_0\,d\mu$ are finite measures, $\rho$ is a finite measure. Suppose, for contradiction, $\rho(X)>0$. Then $\mu(X)>0$ (otherwise $\nu(X)=0$ by $\nu\ll\mu$, forcing $\rho(X)=0$). Let $\varepsilon=\rho(X)/(2\mu(X))>0$, so $\rho(X)>\varepsilon\mu(X)$. Apply Lemma 1 with $\alpha=\rho$, $\beta=\varepsilon\mu$: get $P\in\Sigma$ with $\rho(P)>\varepsilon\mu(P)$ and $\rho(B)\ge\varepsilon\mu(B)$ for all measurable $B\subseteq P$.

We have $\mu(P)>0$: otherwise $\nu(P)=0$, so $0\le\rho(P)\le\nu(P)=0$, contradicting $\rho(P)>\varepsilon\mu(P)=0$.

Let $g'=g_0+\varepsilon\mathbf 1_P$. For $A\in\Sigma$:
$$\int_A g'\,d\mu=\int_Ag_0\,d\mu+\varepsilon\mu(A\cap P)\le\int_Ag_0\,d\mu+\rho(A\cap P)\le\int_Ag_0\,d\mu+\rho(A)=\nu(A).$$
So $g'\in\mathcal F$, but $\int g'\,d\mu=s+\varepsilon\mu(P)>s$, contradicting the definition of $s$. Hence $\rho(X)=0$, so $\rho\equiv0$ (as $0\le\rho(A)\le\rho(X)$), i.e. $\nu(A)=\int_Ag_0\,d\mu$ for all $A\in\Sigma$.

## Step 3: existence in general
Take $X_n$ from Step 1 and define finite measures $\mu_n(A)=\mu(A\cap X_n)$, $\nu_n(A)=\nu(A\cap X_n)$ on $(X,\Sigma)$. If $\mu_n(A)=0$ then $\mu(A\cap X_n)=0$, so $\nu_n(A)=\nu(A\cap X_n)=0$: $\nu_n\ll\mu_n$. By Step 2 there is measurable $g_n:X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\nu_n(A)=\int_A g_n\,d\mu_n$ for all $A$.

For measurable $f\ge0$, $\int f\,d\mu_n=\int f\mathbf 1_{X_n}\,d\mu$: true for indicators by definition, hence for non-negative simple functions by linearity, hence for all $f\ge0$ by MCT applied to simple functions increasing to $f$. Thus $\nu(A\cap X_n)=\int g_n\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu$.

Define $g=\sum_n g_n\mathbf 1_{X_n}$. Each $x$ lies in exactly one $X_n$, so $g(x)=g_n(x)\in[0,\infty)$; $g$ is measurable as a pointwise limit of measurable partial sums; and $g\mathbf 1_{X_n}=g_n\mathbf 1_{X_n}$. For $A\in\Sigma$, by countable additivity of $\nu$ and termwise integration (MCT),
$$\nu(A)=\sum_n\nu(A\cap X_n)=\sum_n\int g\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu=\int\sum_n g\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

## Step 4: uniqueness
Let $g_1,g_2:X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $\int_Ag_1\,d\mu=\int_Ag_2\,d\mu=\nu(A)$ for all $A\in\Sigma$. The set $\{g_1>g_2\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(\{g_1>q\}\cap\{g_2<q\})$ is measurable. Fix $n$ and let $A=X_n\cap\{g_1>g_2\}$. On $A$, $d:=(g_1-g_2)\mathbf 1_A$ is a well-defined non-negative measurable function (values finite) and $g_1\mathbf 1_A=g_2\mathbf 1_A+d$. By additivity,
$$\nu(A)=\int_Ag_1\,d\mu=\int_Ag_2\,d\mu+\int d\,d\mu=\nu(A)+\int d\,d\mu.$$
Since $\nu(A)\le\nu(X_n)<\infty$, we can cancel: $\int d\,d\mu=0$. By Fact 0, $\mu(\{d>0\})=0$, and $\{d>0\}=A$. Hence $\mu(X_n\cap\{g_1>g_2\})=0$ for each $n$; by symmetry $\mu(X_n\cap\{g_2>g_1\})=0$. Therefore $\mu(\{g_1\ne g_2\})\le\sum_n\big[\mu(X_n\cap\{g_1>g_2\})+\mu(X_n\cap\{g_2>g_1\})\big]=0$, i.e. $g_1=g_2$ $\mu$-a.e. $\blacksquare$
